elements.name: Timeout
elements.what: Bound every blocking wait on an external resource or call with a maximum duration, treating expiry as failure.
elements.problem: Unbounded waits on unresponsive dependencies tie up threads and connections, propagating a remote failure into local resource exhaustion and cascading failure.
elements.named_in: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)

elements.name: Circuit Breaker
elements.what: A stateful wrapper around a failure-prone operation that trips open after a failure threshold, rejects calls while open, and probes recovery via a half-open state.
elements.problem: Repeatedly calling a failing dependency wastes resources, slows callers, and hammers the struggling system; the breaker fails fast and gives the dependency time to recover.
elements.named_in: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)

elements.name: Bulkhead
elements.what: Partition resources (thread pools, connection pools, memory) into isolated compartments per client or function so one compartment's exhaustion cannot sink the rest.
elements.problem: A shared pool lets one misbehaving consumer or one slow dependency exhaust capacity for everyone; partitioning contains the damage.
elements.named_in: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)
elements.borderline: Also applied at deployment/cluster level (architecture); the in-process pool-partitioning form is squarely design-level.

elements.name: Steady State
elements.what: For every mechanism that accumulates a resource (log files, cache entries, rows, temp files), pair a mechanism that recycles or purges it, so the program can run indefinitely without human cleanup.
elements.problem: Unbounded accumulation (logs filling disks, caches growing without eviction) eventually kills long-running systems and forces routine human intervention.
elements.named_in: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)
elements.borderline: Close to an operability principle, but kept: it prescribes concrete in-program purge/rotation/eviction mechanisms.

elements.name: Fail Fast
elements.what: Check preconditions and resource availability up front and report failure immediately, rather than doing work that is doomed to fail slowly.
elements.problem: Slow failures consume caller time and system resources; failing before acquiring resources preserves capacity and gives callers fast, actionable errors.
elements.named_in: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)

elements.name: Handshaking
elements.what: Server and client cooperatively signal readiness before work is sent, letting the server refuse or defer new work when saturated.
elements.problem: Protocols that fire requests blindly (plain HTTP) give the server no way to say 'stop sending'; explicit readiness signaling lets components throttle their own load.
elements.named_in: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)

elements.name: Load Shedding
elements.what: When offered load exceeds capacity, deliberately reject or drop a portion of incoming work (cheaply and early) so accepted work still completes within acceptable time.
elements.problem: Accepting all work under overload degrades service for every request and can collapse the system; refusing excess work keeps the remainder healthy.
elements.named_in: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)

elements.name: Back Pressure
elements.what: Propagate 'slow down' signals upstream - via bounded queues, blocking, or demand signaling - so producers cannot outrun consumers.
elements.problem: Unbounded queues hide overload until memory or latency blows up; making queues bounded pushes the overload decision back to the producer, where it can be handled.
elements.named_in: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)

elements.name: Let It Crash
elements.what: On unexpected error, abandon in-process recovery: let the failing unit die immediately and rely on an external mechanism (supervisor, restart) to recreate it in a known-good state.
elements.problem: Defensive recovery code for unanticipated errors is itself error-prone and can leave corrupt state; a clean crash-plus-restart returns to a verified initial state.
elements.named_in: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)
elements.borderline: Erlang-rooted philosophy verging on a design principle; kept because it names a concrete, recurring failure-handling mechanism (crash + supervised restart). Related: Candea & Fox crash-only software.

elements.name: Governor
elements.what: Cap the rate or scope of automated actions (restarts, scale-downs, config pushes) so automation cannot do damage faster than humans can react.
elements.problem: Automation acts at machine speed; a runaway control loop can destroy capacity in seconds, so its actuation rate is deliberately slowed like an engine governor.
elements.named_in: Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. - Nygard (2018)
elements.borderline: Governs ops automation, verging on operations tooling; kept as a named implementable rate-limiting mechanism from a pattern catalog.

elements.name: Recovery Blocks
elements.what: Execute a primary algorithm, validate its result with an acceptance test, and on failure roll back and run an alternate implementation of the same function.
elements.problem: A single implementation may contain residual design faults; structured alternates plus an acceptance test give software fault tolerance within one program.
elements.named_in: System Structure for Software Fault Tolerance - Randell (1975)

elements.name: Checkpoint
elements.what: Periodically save a consistent snapshot of program state so execution can later resume or recover from that point instead of from scratch.
elements.problem: After a failure, recomputing everything from the beginning is too slow or impossible; saved state bounds the work lost to a failure.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Rollback
elements.what: Recover from an error by restoring the system to a previously saved consistent state (a checkpoint) and resuming from there.
elements.problem: An error may have corrupted current state; returning to a known-good earlier state removes the error's effects at the cost of redoing work.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Roll-Forward
elements.what: Recover from an error by advancing the system to a new consistent state ahead of the error point, reconstructing or discarding in-flight work rather than returning to a checkpoint.
elements.problem: Rolling back can be impossible (real-time deadlines, external side effects already visible); moving forward to the next safe state keeps the system live.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Heartbeat
elements.what: A monitored component emits (or answers) a periodic signal; missing beats mark it as failed and trigger recovery.
elements.problem: A silently dead task or peer is indistinguishable from a slow one without an agreed periodic liveness signal and timeout.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Acknowledgement
elements.what: The receiver of a message or request returns an explicit acknowledgement, letting the sender detect loss or peer failure via missing acks within a timeout.
elements.problem: Fire-and-forget communication gives the sender no way to know the peer is alive and the work arrived; acks piggyback failure detection onto normal traffic.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Watchdog Timer
elements.what: A countdown timer that the running software must periodically kick (reset); if the software hangs and the timer expires, hardware or a monitor forces a reset or corrective action.
elements.problem: A hung or livelocked program cannot report its own failure; an independent timer converts 'stopped making progress' into a detectable, recoverable event.
elements.named_in: Making Embedded Systems: Design Patterns for Great Software - White (2024)

elements.name: Riding Over Transients
elements.what: Deliberately ignore errors that are momentary and self-clearing, acting only when an error persists or recurs beyond a threshold.
elements.problem: Reacting instantly to every transient glitch triggers needless recovery actions that cost more than the fault itself; filtering separates transient from persistent faults.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Leaky Bucket Counter
elements.what: An error counter incremented on each fault and decremented ('leaked') periodically; recovery escalates only when the count crosses a threshold, i.e. errors arrive faster than they drain.
elements.problem: Distinguishing an acceptable background rate of transient errors from a persistent fault requires rate, not count; the leak encodes the acceptable rate. Distinct from the leaky-bucket traffic shaper.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Marked Data
elements.what: Tag data elements known or suspected to be erroneous so subsequent processing can skip, repair, or handle them specially instead of propagating the corruption.
elements.problem: Deleting bad data may be worse than keeping it; an explicit corruption mark contains the error while preserving structure and audit trail.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Escalation
elements.what: When a recovery action fails to clear an error, escalate to a progressively more drastic action (retry -> restart task -> restart process -> reboot) up a defined ladder.
elements.problem: No single recovery action handles all faults; an ordered ladder bounds recovery time while preferring the least disruptive action that works.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Quarantine
elements.what: Isolate a faulty element from the rest of the system - stop routing work to it, fence its outputs - so its errors cannot spread while diagnosis or recovery proceeds.
elements.problem: A faulty unit that keeps participating spreads corrupt data and secondary failures; active isolation contains the damage.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)
elements.borderline: Presumes isolatable units, which shades architectural; kept because in-process quarantine (disabling a worker, fencing a plugin) is implementable in one component.

elements.name: Error Handler
elements.what: Concentrate error-processing logic in dedicated handler components/blocks separate from normal-flow code, invoked when errors are detected.
elements.problem: Error handling interleaved with mainline logic is duplicated, inconsistent, and untestable; separating it gives one place to get recovery right.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Restart
elements.what: Recover from an unhandled or unrecoverable error by reinitializing the affected unit (task, process, component, or whole program) to its known-good initial state.
elements.problem: Some errors leave state too corrupt to repair in place; restarting from verified initial conditions is the recovery of last resort with predictable cost.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Software Rejuvenation
elements.what: Proactively restart or reinitialize a long-running process on a schedule or on resource-degradation signals, before software aging (leaks, fragmentation, drift) causes failure.
elements.problem: Long-running processes accumulate degradation that eventually causes outages at uncontrolled moments; planned rejuvenation converts that into cheap, scheduled downtime.
elements.named_in: Software Rejuvenation: Analysis, Module and Applications - Huang, Kintala, Kolettis, Fulton (1995)

elements.name: Correcting Audits
elements.what: Routinely scan in-memory or stored data for structural and semantic errors and repair them (rebuild links, reset invalid fields) as they are found.
elements.problem: Data errors accumulate silently from faults elsewhere and eventually trigger failures; active auditing finds and corrects them before they are used.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Complete Parameter Checking
elements.what: Validate all parameters and inputs at component boundaries every time, detecting errors close to their source at the cost of some performance.
elements.problem: Faults manifest as bad values crossing interfaces; checking at the boundary shortens fault latency and stops propagation into the component.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Checksum
elements.what: Store or transmit a redundant value computed from data (sum, CRC, hash) and recompute it on use to detect corruption.
elements.problem: Memory, storage, and transmission silently corrupt bits; a cheap redundant check converts silent corruption into a detectable error. CRC and stronger digests are folded here as variants.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)

elements.name: Error-Correcting Codes
elements.what: Encode data with structured redundancy so that a bounded number of bit errors can be not only detected but corrected on read/receive.
elements.problem: When retransmission or re-read is impossible or too slow, correction must come from the data itself; redundant encodings trade space for self-healing data. Code-family variants (Hamming, Reed-Solomon, LDPC) stay in the algorithmics zoo.
elements.named_in: Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes - Hamming (1950)

elements.name: N-Version Programming
elements.what: Run N independently developed implementations of the same specification and adjudicate their outputs by a voter to mask residual design faults.
elements.problem: Identical redundant copies share design faults; diverse implementations plus majority voting tolerate faults no single version can. The voter/voting mechanism (Hanmer: Voting) is folded here.
elements.named_in: The N-Version Approach to Fault-Tolerant Software - Avizienis (1985)
elements.borderline: Development-process-heavy (independent teams, common spec), but the runtime N-version-plus-voter execution is implementable inside one program; kept with tag rather than parked.

elements.name: Deferrable Work
elements.what: Classify work as essential vs deferrable and, under overload, postpone deferrable tasks (audits, housekeeping, statistics) until load subsides.
elements.problem: Under overload every cycle matters; explicitly deferring non-urgent work preserves capacity for revenue/critical processing without dropping it entirely.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)
elements.borderline: An overload policy inside one component; near operational policy but named and mechanically implementable (priority demotion, deferral queues).

elements.name: Fresh Work Before Stale
elements.what: Under overload, serve the newest requests first (LIFO) because the oldest queued requests have likely already timed out or been abandoned by their requesters.
elements.problem: FIFO under sustained overload spends capacity on requests whose callers have given up, so nobody gets service; newest-first lets at least recent requesters succeed.
elements.named_in: Patterns for Fault Tolerant Software - Hanmer (2007)
elements.borderline: A queue-discipline choice shading into policy; kept as a named, implementable overload mechanism (cf. adaptive LIFO in later SRE literature).

elements.name: Retry with Exponential Backoff and Jitter
elements.what: Retry a failed operation a bounded number of times, doubling the wait between attempts and randomizing (jittering) it to avoid synchronized retry storms.
elements.problem: Immediate or fixed-interval retries from many clients synchronize into load spikes that prolong the outage they respond to; capped attempts (Hanmer: Limit Retries, folded here) prevent infinite retry loops.
elements.named_in: Timeouts, Retries, and Backoff with Jitter - Brooker, AWS Builders' Library (2019)

elements.name: Retry Budget
elements.what: Cap retries globally as a fraction of primary requests (e.g. retries may add at most 10% extra load), disabling retry when the budget is exhausted.
elements.problem: Per-request retry limits still multiply load during a broad outage; a system-wide budget prevents retry amplification from turning partial failure into total overload.
elements.named_in: Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems - Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy eds. (2016)

elements.name: Token Bucket
elements.what: Tokens accrue in a bucket at a fixed rate up to a capacity; each admitted unit of work consumes tokens, allowing bursts up to the bucket size while enforcing a long-term average rate.
elements.problem: Pure fixed-rate policing forbids legitimate bursts; the bucket capacity encodes an allowed burst while still bounding sustained throughput.
elements.named_in: Computer Networks, 3rd ed. - Tanenbaum (1996)

elements.name: Leaky Bucket
elements.what: Arriving work enters a bounded bucket that drains at a constant rate; overflow is rejected, converting bursty input into a smooth constant-rate output.
elements.problem: Downstream stages that cannot absorb bursts need arrival smoothing; the bucket enforces a hard output rate regardless of input burstiness. Distinct from Hanmer's Leaky Bucket Counter (error counting).
elements.named_in: New Directions in Communications (or Which Way to the Information Age?) - Turner (1986)

elements.name: Sliding-Window Rate Limiting
elements.what: Admit a request only if the count of requests in the trailing time window is below a limit, tracked by a per-window counter, a timestamp log, or a weighted blend of adjacent windows.
elements.problem: API quotas expressed as 'N requests per interval' need a counting mechanism; window variants trade memory and precision against boundary-burst artifacts. Granularity decision: the three window variants are folded into this one element; token bucket and leaky bucket stay separate mechanisms.
elements.named_in: System Design Interview - An Insider's Guide - Xu (2020)

elements.name: Timer Wheel
elements.what: A circular array of time slots, each holding the timers expiring in that tick; a pointer advances per tick, making start/stop/expire O(1) for large timer populations.
elements.problem: Sorted timer lists degrade with tens of thousands of pending timeouts (protocol stacks, event systems); the wheel bounds per-tick work regardless of timer count. Hashed/hierarchical forms are variants, not separate elements.
elements.named_in: Hashed and Hierarchical Timing Wheels: Data Structures for the Efficient Implementation of a Timer Facility - Varghese, Lauck (1987)

elements.name: Throttle
elements.what: Ensure a function or action executes at most once per interval, discarding or coalescing invocations that arrive faster.
elements.problem: High-frequency event streams (scroll, sensor readings, status updates) would trigger expensive handlers far faster than useful; throttling caps the execution rate while keeping periodic updates.
elements.named_in: Debouncing and Throttling Explained Through Examples - Corbacho, CSS-Tricks (2016)

elements.name: Debounce
elements.what: Suppress rapid repeated triggers by acting only after the input has been quiet (or stable) for a defined interval, collapsing a burst into one event.
elements.problem: Mechanical switches bounce and users type in bursts; acting on every raw transition causes spurious repeated actions, so the mechanism waits for the signal to settle. Overlaps the embedded scout (hardware debouncing) by design.
elements.named_in: A Guide to Debouncing - Ganssle (2004)

elements.name: Lease
elements.what: Grant a right (cache validity, lock, ownership) only for a bounded term that the holder must renew; expiry automatically revokes the right without contacting the possibly-failed holder.
elements.problem: Permanent grants to a crashed or partitioned holder block everyone forever; bounding the grant by time makes failure recovery a matter of waiting out the term.
elements.named_in: Leases: An Efficient Fault-Tolerant Mechanism for Distributed File Cache Consistency - Gray, Cheriton (1989)

elements.name: Fencing Token
elements.what: Attach a monotonically increasing token to each lock/lease grant; resources reject requests bearing a token older than one already seen, fencing off stale holders.
elements.problem: A paused or partitioned client may act on an expired lease it believes it still holds; token comparison at the resource makes such zombie writes rejectable.
elements.named_in: Designing Data-Intensive Applications - Kleppmann (2017)

elements.name: Time to Live (TTL)
elements.what: Attach a lifetime to a datum, message, or entry; holders treat it as invalid (and evict or drop it) once the lifetime elapses.
elements.problem: Stale cache entries, undead packets, and orphaned records need a self-destruct mechanism that works without coordination; a carried lifetime bounds staleness and loops.
elements.named_in: RFC 791: Internet Protocol - Postel (1981)
elements.borderline: Often just a protocol field or config knob; kept for the recurring in-program expiry mechanism (cache TTLs, message expiry, session lifetime).

elements.name: Idempotent Receiver
elements.what: The receiver detects and discards duplicate requests/messages - typically via a client-supplied unique key remembered across calls - so retries and redeliveries have exactly-once effect.
elements.problem: At-least-once delivery and client retries inevitably duplicate messages; deduplicating at the receiver makes retry-based recovery safe for non-idempotent operations.
elements.named_in: Enterprise Integration Patterns - Hohpe, Woolf (2003)

elements.name: Hedged Request
elements.what: After a brief delay (e.g. the 95th-percentile latency), send the same request to a second replica and use whichever response returns first, cancelling the other.
elements.problem: Tail latency of a fan-out is dominated by the slowest straggler; a small number of duplicate requests cuts tail latency dramatically for modest extra load.
elements.named_in: The Tail at Scale - Dean, Barroso (2013)
elements.borderline: Targets multi-replica distributed systems, but is a purely client-side implementable mechanism; kept per charter with tag.

elements.name: Deadline Propagation
elements.what: Carry an absolute deadline (or remaining budget) with each request and pass it down the call chain; every stage checks it and aborts work whose deadline has already passed.
elements.problem: Independent per-hop timeouts let deep call chains do work the original caller has already abandoned; a propagated deadline stops wasted work everywhere at once.
elements.named_in: Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems - Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy eds. (2016)
elements.borderline: Spans a call chain across services, but each hop implements it locally (check-and-forward); kept as design-level with tag.

elements.name: Serial Number Arithmetic
elements.what: Compare fixed-width, wrapping sequence numbers using modular half-range rules so ordering remains correct across wraparound.
elements.problem: Naive comparison of wrapping counters (TCP sequence numbers, DNS serials, timestamps) breaks at rollover; half-range modular comparison keeps 'newer than' well-defined.
elements.named_in: RFC 1982: Serial Number Arithmetic - Elz, Bush (1996)

elements.name: Design by Contract
elements.what: Specify each routine's obligations as executable preconditions, postconditions, and class invariants, checked at runtime, with blame assigned by which side's clause failed.
elements.problem: Informal interface expectations cause misuse and blur responsibility for failures; executable contracts document, verify, and localize violations at the boundary where they occur.
elements.named_in: Object-Oriented Software Construction - Meyer (1988)

elements.name: Runtime Assertion
elements.what: Embed executable checks of conditions the programmer believes must hold; a failed check aborts or reports immediately, at the point of the impossible state.
elements.problem: Latent programmer errors surface far from their cause; assertions convert silent invariant violations into immediate, located failures. The mechanism, not the per-language assert keyword, is the element.
elements.named_in: Code Complete, 2nd ed. - McConnell (2004)

elements.name: Stack Canary
elements.what: Place a secret guard value between a stack frame's buffers and its control data (return address); verify it before returning, aborting if a buffer overflow overwrote it.
elements.problem: Stack buffer overflows silently overwrite return addresses, enabling control-flow hijack; a checked sentinel converts the overwrite into a detected crash.
elements.named_in: StackGuard: Automatic Adaptive Detection and Prevention of Buffer-Overflow Attacks - Cowan et al. (1998)

elements.name: Constant-Time Comparison
elements.what: Compare secret-dependent data (MACs, tokens, passwords hashes) with an algorithm whose running time and memory access pattern are independent of the data values.
elements.problem: Early-exit comparison leaks how many leading bytes matched through timing, letting attackers recover secrets byte by byte; data-independent execution closes the side channel.
elements.named_in: BearSSL: Constant-Time Crypto - Pornin (living)

elements.name: Secure Zeroization
elements.what: Erase sensitive data (keys, passwords) from memory using an operation the compiler cannot optimize away, immediately after last use.
elements.problem: Ordinary memset before free is dead-store-eliminated by optimizers, leaving secrets recoverable from memory dumps, swap, or reuse; guaranteed-erase primitives close the gap.
elements.named_in: The CERT C Coding Standard, 2nd ed. - Seacord (2014)

elements.name: Supervisor
elements.what: A component whose only job is to monitor child workers and apply a declared restart strategy (one-for-one, one-for-all, escalation to its own supervisor) when they crash.
elements.problem: Let-it-crash needs someone to do the restarting; a hierarchy of supervisors turns individual crashes into localized, policy-driven recovery instead of whole-program failure.
elements.named_in: OTP Design Principles (Erlang/OTP documentation) - Ericsson (living)

elements.name: Error Kernel
elements.what: Keep the irreplaceable state and critical logic in a small, maximally simple core, delegating risky or failure-prone work to expendable child components that can crash and be restarted.
elements.problem: If valuable state lives where risky work happens, every failure threatens it; pushing risk to the leaves lets crashes stay cheap while the kernel stays reliable.
elements.named_in: Reactive Design Patterns - Kuhn, Hanafee, Allen (2017)

elements.name: Rate-Monotonic Scheduling
elements.what: Assign fixed priorities to periodic tasks inversely to their periods (shortest period = highest priority), which is optimal among fixed-priority schemes and admits analytic schedulability bounds.
elements.problem: Hard real-time systems must guarantee deadlines before runtime; rate-monotonic priority assignment plus utilization-bound analysis gives a provable admission test. Overlaps the embedded scout's territory; kept per the scheduling-and-time charter.
elements.named_in: Scheduling Algorithms for Multiprogramming in a Hard-Real-Time Environment - Liu, Layland (1973)

elements.name: Earliest Deadline First
elements.what: Dynamically dispatch the ready task whose absolute deadline is nearest, achieving full processor utilization for schedulable periodic task sets.
elements.problem: Fixed priorities waste capacity (utilization bound below 100%); deadline-driven dynamic priority reclaims it, at the cost of less predictable overload behavior. Overlaps the embedded scout; kept per the scheduling-and-time charter.
elements.named_in: Scheduling Algorithms for Multiprogramming in a Hard-Real-Time Environment - Liu, Layland (1973)

parked_architecture.name: Failover
parked_architecture.why: Hanmer pattern; switching service to a redundant unit is primarily a system-level structure/tactic (per charter directive: park if system-level).

parked_architecture.name: Redundancy (spatial/temporal/informational)
parked_architecture.why: Hanmer architectural pattern; provisioning redundant units is an availability tactic / system structure, not an in-program mechanism.

parked_architecture.name: Units of Mitigation
parked_architecture.why: Hanmer architectural pattern; defines the system's recovery-unit decomposition - a structural statement.

parked_architecture.name: Error Containment Barrier
parked_architecture.why: Hanmer architectural pattern; primarily prescribes structural boundaries for error propagation across the system.

parked_architecture.name: Someone in Charge
parked_architecture.why: Hanmer architectural pattern; assigns system-wide responsibility for fault-handling actions - structural/organizational.

parked_architecture.name: Fault Observer
parked_architecture.why: Hanmer pattern; a system-wide component collecting and publishing fault reports - topology-level.

parked_architecture.name: System Monitor
parked_architecture.why: Hanmer detection pattern; a dedicated monitoring component watching the rest of the system - system-level structure.

parked_architecture.name: Maintenance Interface
parked_architecture.why: Hanmer pattern; a separate management/maintenance channel beside the application interface - architectural interface decision.

parked_architecture.name: Health Check (endpoint)
parked_architecture.why: Per charter directive; a service-exposed liveness/readiness probe is a system/operations integration construct (cf. heartbeat, which stays design-level).

parked_architecture.name: Decoupling Middleware
parked_architecture.why: Nygard stability pattern; choosing middleware topology to decouple systems is architectural.

parked_architecture.name: Graceful Degradation
parked_architecture.why: System-level quality tactic (SRE / Bass availability tactics); realized by design elements like load shedding and circuit breaker but itself a system property.

parked_architecture.name: Process Pairs
parked_architecture.why: Gray (1985, Tandem); primary/backup process structure with takeover - system-level redundancy organization.

parked_architecture.name: Triple Modular Redundancy (TMR)
parked_architecture.why: Lyons & Vanderkulk (1962); hardware/system-level redundancy with voting; software analog covered by n-version-programming element.

parked_architecture.name: Saga / Compensating Transaction
parked_architecture.why: Garcia-Molina & Salem (1987); long-lived transaction structure spanning services - architecture-level failure handling (flagging for Phase 3; may also belong to a persistence scout).

parked_architecture.name: Shed Work at Periphery
parked_architecture.why: Hanmer overload pattern; prescribes WHERE in the system to shed load (at the edge) - a placement/topology statement; the mechanism itself is the load-shedding element.

excluded_notable.name: Test Harness
excluded_notable.why: Nygard stability pattern, but it is testing infrastructure/practice, not a runtime design mechanism.

excluded_notable.name: Software Update / Small Patches
excluded_notable.why: Hanmer fault-treatment patterns; deployment/maintenance process, not in-program mechanisms.

excluded_notable.name: Minimize Human Intervention / Maximize Human Participation
excluded_notable.why: Hanmer patterns; human-factors and operations principles.

excluded_notable.name: Root Cause Analysis / Revise Procedure / Reproducible Error / Let Sleeping Dogs Lie
excluded_notable.why: Hanmer fault-treatment patterns; engineering/ops process guidance.

excluded_notable.name: Routine Audits / Routine Exercises / Routine Maintenance
excluded_notable.why: Hanmer detection patterns of the operational-practice kind (scheduled ops activities), unlike Correcting Audits which is an in-program mechanism.

excluded_notable.name: Realistic Threshold / Existing Metrics
excluded_notable.why: Hanmer detection patterns that are parameter-tuning guidance rather than mechanisms.

excluded_notable.name: Defensive Programming
excluded_notable.why: Umbrella practice (McConnell); its concrete mechanisms are cataloged individually (assertions, parameter checking, fail fast).

excluded_notable.name: Fail-Safe Defaults
excluded_notable.why: Saltzer & Schroeder security design principle - a principle, not an implementable mechanism.

excluded_notable.name: Chaos Engineering / fault injection in production
excluded_notable.why: Practice/discipline (Principles of Chaos Engineering), pass-7 process territory.

notes: Coverage: Nygard 2nd-ed ch5 stability patterns fully swept (Timeouts, Circuit Breaker, Bulkheads, Steady State, Fail Fast, Let It Crash, Handshaking, Test Harness->excluded, Decoupling Middleware->parked, Shed Load, Create Back Pressure, Governor). Hanmer swept via live ch4 summary + index-level confirmation; sub-patterns folded: Limit Retries -> retry element; Voting -> n-version-programming; Return to Reference Point / What to Save / Remote Storage / Data Reset -> checkpoint family (noted, not enumerated); Queue for Resources folds into general queueing (dataflow scout). Rate-limiter granularity decision: token bucket, leaky bucket, and window-based counting are three genuinely distinct mechanisms = 3 elements, with the fixed/sliding-log/sliding-counter window variants folded into one; Hanmer's Leaky Bucket Counter kept separate (error-rate detector, not traffic shaper). N-version programming: INCLUDED borderline (runtime voter implementable) rather than parked. Failover and health check parked per charter.
